title: Looks like: 〜そう(appearance), 〜がる, 〜やすい/にくい, 〜ながら

grammarPoints.rule: Take an adjective, cut its tail, add そう — and you are reporting how something LOOKS before you have tried it. おいしい → おいしそう: it looks tasty, says the eye, not the tongue. たかい → たかそう, looks expensive. The い goes; そう sits on the bare stem. Two irregulars, learned now while the rule is fresh: いい becomes よさそう (looks good), and ない becomes なさそう (looks like there isn't). What you get behaves like a な-adjective: おいしそうな りょうり, a tasty-looking dish. The whole point of the form is the gap between looks and knowledge — you say おいしそう BEFORE the first bite; after it, you just say おいしい.

examples.ja: この りょうりは おいしそう。
その とけいは たかそう。
この ほんは おもしろそう。
きょうは てんきが よさそう。

antiPattern.ja: この りょうりは おいしいそう。
antiPattern.why: そう sits on the STEM — the い has to go: おいしそう. (Keeping the い builds a different word you will meet much later; for now it is simply not the looks-like form.)

grammarPoints.rule: On a verb, そう takes the ます-stem — the same stem you have used since module 7 — and means it looks about to happen: ふる → ふりそう, looks like rain. おちる → おちそう, about to fall. The feel is an event leaning forward; you say it while there is still time to grab the cup. Negatives go two ways and both are worth having: あめは ふらなさそう (it doesn't look like rain) and あめは ふりそうにない (there's no sign of it raining) — the second is the stronger, flatter denial. Both are recognition-first here; production comes with use.

examples.ja: かばんから さいふが おちそう。
examples.en: Your wallet looks about to fall out of your bag.

examples.ja: えいがが はじまりそう。
examples.en: The film looks about to start.

examples.ja: あめは ふりそうにない。

antiPattern.why: the looks-like そう rides the ます-stem: ふり + そう. On the dictionary form it stops being about looks at all — ふりそう is what the sky shows you.

grammarPoints.rule: Japanese is honest about other minds: you know what YOU want, but you can only READ what others want. That is why 「おとうとは いきたい」 sounds off — たい is first-person interior. For third person, がる turns the feeling into visible behavior: いきたい → いきたがる, "he's acting like he wants to go." Almost always in ている, because the behavior is ongoing: おとうとは こうえんに いきたがっている。 The same がる works straight on emotion adjectives — こわい → こわがる (to act scared), はずかしい → はずかしがる (to act embarrassed). Cut the い, add がる, and the private feeling becomes the public verb of showing it. This closes a door N5 deliberately left shut: now you can finally say what somebody ELSE wants.

examples.ja: おとうとは こうえんに いきたがっている。
examples.en: My little brother wants to go to the park.

examples.ja: いもうとは あたらしい くつを かいたがっている。
examples.en: My little sister wants to buy new shoes.

examples.ja: ねこは そとに でたがっている。
examples.en: The cat wants to go outside.

antiPattern.ja: おとうとは こうえんに いきたい。
antiPattern.why: たい is first-person interior — you can't feel your brother's wanting from the inside. What you CAN see is the wanting-behavior: いきたがっている。

grammarPoints.rule: Stem + やすい: easy to. Stem + にくい: hard to. The same attachment site as たい (module 13) — よむ → よみやすい (easy to read), わかる → わかりにくい (hard to follow). And here is the payoff of building adjectives out of adjectives: the result IS an i-adjective, so everything you know about i-adjectives applies unchanged — よみやすかった, わかりにくくない, たべやすくて。 It is judgment about the THING, not about you: この じしょは つかいやすい praises the dictionary, not your skill. Pick the stem, pick the half, and the language does the rest with machinery you have owned for twenty modules.

examples.ja: この じしょは つかいやすい。
examples.en: This dictionary is easy to use.

examples.ja: この ことばは おぼえにくい。
examples.en: This word is hard to memorise.

examples.ja: ミカの せつめいは わかりやすい。
examples.en: Mika's explanations are easy to follow.

examples.ja: この みちは あるきやすかった。
examples.en: This road was easy to walk.

antiPattern.ja: この じしょは つかうやすい。
antiPattern.why: やすい rides the ます-stem, exactly like たい: つかい + やすい. The dictionary form never takes the attachment.

grammarPoints.rule: Stem + ながら: doing one thing WHILE doing another. おんがくを ききながら しゅくだいを する — homework, with music behind it. Same attachment site again: the ます-stem, nothing new to learn about the shape. One rule of meaning that English hides: the ながら-half is the BACKGROUND, and the sentence's real point comes second. 「たべながら テレビを みる」 is watching TV (main), over food (background); flip the halves and you flip what matters. Both actions belong to the same person — ながら never joins two different people's doings.

examples.ja: おんがくを ききながら しゅくだいを する。
examples.en: I do my homework while listening to music.

examples.ja: テレビを みながら ごはんを たべる。
examples.en: I eat dinner while watching TV.

examples.ja: あるきながら はなす。

antiPattern.ja: おんがくを きくながら しゅくだいを する。
antiPattern.why: ながら rides the ます-stem like every attachment in this module: きき + ながら. The dictionary form doesn't take it.

lessons.title: Review — looks, on both word classes

lessons.title: 「いきたがっている」 — reading other minds

lessons.title: 「ききながら」 — two things, one person
lessons.focus: Stem + ながら runs a background action under the main one — and すぎる comes back for harder spends

beats.stem: おんがくを ききながら、
beats.answer: しゅくだいを する
options: しゅくだいを する
beats.en: While listening to music, I do my homework
beats.explanation: the ながら-half is the background (ききながら); whichever verb comes SECOND is the sentence's real point — here, doing homework. した just skips the ながら-frame with a bare past. テレビを みる would make watching TV the point instead, forgetting the music.

beats.en: This road is easy to walk

beats.ja: おんがくを ききながら あるく。
beats.en: I walk while listening to music
This road is easy to walk
beats.explanation: やすい judges the road itself. ながら would need a second action happening at the same time. あるく alone carries no judgment at all.

beats.ja: この じしょは わかりやすい。

beats.ja: この みちは きけん。
beats.en: This road is dangerous

beats.stem: その みちより、この みちの ほうが
beats.en: This road is safer than that one
beats.explanation: あんぜん names the safety itself. きけん would flip the meaning to danger. たかい is a real word, just the wrong one — 'expensive,' nothing to do with safety.

beats.tail: けど、あの せつめいは わかりやすい。
beats.en: This explanation is hard to follow, but that explanation is easy to follow
beats.explanation: にくい makes the hard-to version, and the contrast with わかりやすい in the second half forces it. おぼえにくい is the right suffix on the wrong verb — hard to MEMORISE, not hard to follow. わかった is just the plain past 'understood,' no difficulty judgment at all.
